### 8.1.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Faced with the destructive reality of computational linguistic manipulation, the doctrines of civil and public law must be radically reconstructed (Hildebrandt, 2015; Calo, 2014). Hitherto, conventional contract law has been rooted in the liberal philosophical assumption that contracting parties maintain an equality of arms and a pure autonomy of will (Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*); Weizenbaum, 1976). However, when a technology corporation deploys a generative AI system capable of hyper-personalized manipulation through the exploitation of linguistic structures and user psychological vulnerabilities, this assumption of equality collapses entirely (Zuboff, 2019; Farahany, 2023). Under the framework of Indonesian positive law—specifically Article 1320 in conjunction with Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)—an agreement or contract may be annulled if there is a defect of will (*wilsgebreke*) caused by fraud (*bedrog*), mistake (*dwaling*), or psychological duress / undue influence (*bedreiging / misbruik van omstandigheden*) (Subekti, 2014). In the era of artificial intelligence, fraud and misrepresentation no longer manifest as spoken falsehoods consciously uttered by biological legal subjects, but rather as algorithmic misrepresentation—a distortion of reality automatically generated by large language models programmed to pursue commercial engagement metrics with utter disregard for the user's mental integrity (Floridi, 2013).

Furthermore, the international regulatory landscape has begun to move toward the recognition of this cognitive protection (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689). The advent of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act 2024—specifically the provisions in Article 5, which explicitly prohibit AI practices that deploy subliminal or manipulative techniques to materially distort a person's behavior in a manner that causes or is likely to cause physical or psychological harm—marks a new chapter in the history of technology regulation (Hildebrandt, 2015). This regulation recognizes that freedom of thought and cognitive integrity constitute the final bulwark of human dignity (Jonas, 1979; Levinas, 1961). Yet, normative prohibitions of this nature will lack effective enforcement teeth unless supported by objective empirical evidentiary instruments (Coulthard & Johnson, 2007). This is precisely where the methodology of Computational Linguistic Forensic Auditing serves as a vital legal evidentiary bridge. When a plaintiff seeks damages for material or immaterial losses resulting from psychological manipulation by a commercial AI system, a forensic linguistic audit report—dissecting the model's latent space, lexical entrainment patterns, and pragmatic distortions within conversational transcripts—will be accepted by the panel of judges as valid documentary evidence and scientifically verifiable expert testimony (Article 1866 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*); HIR/RBg).

In the realm of personal data protection, the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (UU PDP), harmonized with the principles of the *GDPR* in the European Union, provides a foundational baseline through the data subject's right to object to decisions based solely on automated processing (*automated individual decision-making*), including profiling that produces legal effects or similarly significantly impacts the data subject (EU Regulation 2016/679). Nevertheless, this protection remains confined to the dimensions of structured personal data, and does not yet fully reach the cognitive-semantic dimensions exploited by generative language models (Farahany, 2023). Consequently, a novel doctrinal construction is required to elevate the right to mental integrity and the freedom of cognitive autonomy into non-derogable constitutional rights (Jonas, 1979). 

The state, through its positive obligations, must mandate regular linguistic and psychological forensic audits for any high-capacity generative AI system before it is permitted to operate within the public space of the national jurisdiction (Calo, 2014; EU AI Act, 2024). Such audits should no longer merely examine source code security or data storage encryption, but must test persuasive toxicity capacity, potential lexical manipulation, and the model's propensity for psychological exploitation of vulnerable groups (Weizenbaum, 1976; Zuboff, 2019). Armed with this robust doctrinal framework, the law will no longer limp behind the pace of destructive technological innovation, but will stand resolutely as the guardian of human dignity—ensuring that language, the crown jewel of human civilization, is not reduced by corporate algorithms into a silent weapon used to enslave the consciousness of its very users (Habermas, 1984; Levinas, 1961).
